structure: Single-grade Vermont draft framework document (Grade 1 - People, Places, and the Environment). Front matter: header banner, title/theme, Overview narrative, Looking Back/Looking Ahead, Inquiry rationale and contact. Inquiry Process block: 'Inquiry Process (K-12)' statement, a banded list of C3 indicators (K-2) and overarching grade themes. Body is organized by four subject sections (Civics, Economics, Geography, History), each with a 'Theme:' line, C3-strand headings (e.g. Civic and Political Institutions; Economic Decision Making; Geographic Representations; Change, Continuity, and Context) followed by the C3 indicator codes (D2.<Dim>.<n>.K-2). Each strand/indicator group is followed by a 2-column table (R1 headers 'Sample C3 Indicator Connections' | 'Sample Content Connections'; R2 cells hold C1 = 'Students will...' expectations, C2 = bulleted sample content). Rows continued over pages start with 'Continue'. Each subject ends with a 'Resources' list of suggested lessons/inquiries (C3 IDM, iCivics, PBS, etc.). The vermont.gov banner and running headers are furniture. No state-specific standard codes; the D2 C3 codes and the 'Students will' expectations are the standards. Labeling: titles/themes/strand headings/codes/inquiry indicators/'Students will' cells = standards; Sample Content Connections cells, Overview narrative and Resources = examples; Looking Back/Ahead, inquiry rationale, scope notes = backup.
issues: Inquiry Process / C3-indicator / Priority Performance Indicator lists that name a band (K-2, 3-5, 6-8) or K-12 are labeled with that band (shared inquiry skills); everything else is labeled with this file's single grade, per the state guide (one document = one grade).
Resource entries that wrap across pages are split into two units (second unit continues the first); both are labeled examples.
'Note:' lines saying an indicator is not addressed in this grade, and the 'Looking Back/Looking Ahead' paragraphs, are labeled backup.
u29-u30: D2.Civ.6.K-2 text split in extraction ('Authority.' tail is u30).
u115 and u114: Economic Interdependence resource says it is a 2nd grade inquiry adaptable for younger students; kept as examples for grade 1.
u91, u130, u158, u183, u201: C2 cells sometimes begin with an unbulleted sub-heading or a long 'Community Action Examples' list; labeled examples as one unit.

Grade 1 – People, Places, and the Environment (Draft)
Overview

In grade 1, students will learn how they are connected to the world around them and develop a deeper understanding of how diverse cultures, values, and beliefs help to shape the world in which we live. Students will further develop a sense of purpose and empathy regarding their role and the role of other citizens within the community and world. As a global citizen, it is developmentally appropriate for students to identify similarities and differences from others (cultural, likes and dislikes, gender, skin color, hair, and eye color). Best practice is having materials and visuals that are representative of people, cultures, and the community in which they live. They will have the opportunity to look for ways that they can be civic-minded and make change happen within their own classroom, school, and community. Students will develop an understanding of how basic economic concepts influence people, places, and the environment. They will learn that people not only use the environment to meet their needs and wants but also that the environment often dictates where and how people choose to live. Students will continue building group skills, including roles, rules, voicing an opinion, and conflict resolution skills with adult support. They will enhance their knowledge of spatial awareness of their surroundings by furthering the use of geographic representations, tools, and terminology to process information about the world around them. Students will continue to compare life in the past to life today as they study the contributions of historical figures and how those figures have helped shape and change various communities and environments across the globe.
Looking Back and Looking Ahead
Kindergarten – Me and My Community

In kindergarten, students explored topics that affect them and their personal environments, learned basic citizenship skills, and engaged in learning about themselves, their schools, their cities/towns, and individuals in their local communities.
Contact: Martha Deiss, Curriculum & Instruction Division, at Martha.Deiss@vermont.gov
Looking Ahead
2nd Grade – The Americas

In grade 2, students will expand on their understanding of the concept of community by exploring past and present interactions between groups of people in Central America, North America, South America, and the Caribbean. Students will explain continuities and differences among cultures, governments, traditions, and available resources to investigate how individuals work together while acknowledging different perspectives and cultivating empathy.
Inquiry

Why inquiry? Using inquiry as an instructional model for the teaching of social studies allows students to authentically ask questions, search for and analyze evidence, and provide explanations and arguments to challenges facing their world.

The inquiry instructional model is driven by authentic questions or problems that have relevance for children. Students learn content, skills, and dispositions as they seek answers to questions and as they apply their learning to take informed action. Pioneered by Dewey (1938), inquiry is an attempt to make classroom experiences feel more like the authentic, curiosity-driven experiences that motivate learning outside of school. (Using Inquiry to Prepare Students for College, Career, and Civic Life, elementary edition, p. 22)

The Inquiry Arc is defined in Dimension 1 (questioning) of the College, Career, and Civic Life (C3) Framework for Social Studies State Standards. In this Framework, Dimension 3 (evidence sourcing), and Dimension 4 (communicating), as well as some evidence indicators found within Dimension 2 – History, have been combined with Dimension 1 into a singular Inquiry Process, as evidenced below. This Inquiry Process begins in the elementary grades and increases in depth and complexity as it spans through high school, preparing students to spiral their learning and skill acquisition in the social studies for college and career readiness.
Inquiry Process: Students act as social scientists as they ask questions, think critically, solve problems, and share conclusions.

Sample C3 Indicator Connections
Sample Content Connections

Students will identify local community and government leaders that have roles and responsibilities to provide services for their community members. Students will be able to explain how communities have rules and people in charge to keep things fair and help everyone get what they need.

• Different people serve in appointed and/or elected roles in governments. • Leaders have different roles and responsibilities. • Governments represent the needs of the people, create and enforce laws, and help to resolve conflicts. • Governments provide services (education, roads, parks, public safety). • Civic identity is shaped by symbolic figures, places, and events. • People elect officials to represent them. • Citizens help to form their government. • Voting determines who will be president and vice president. • The president is the leader of the country, and the vice president is second in charge. • Individuals work together to respect and uphold the rights of the self and others in the community. • Learners in the classroom community have rights (feeling safe, belonging, learning).
Civic Virtues and Democratic Principles: Applying Civic Virtues and Democratic Principles
D2.Civ.7.K-2. Apply civic virtues when participating in school settings.
D2.Civ.8.K-2. Describe democratic principles such as equality, fairness, and respect for legitimate authority and rules.
D2.Civ.9.K-2. Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions while responding attentively to others when addressing ideas and making decisions as a group.
D2.Civ.10.K-2. Compare their own point of view with others’ perspectives.

Sample Content Connections

Students will understand that children, families, and communities exhibit cultural similarities and differences. Students will be able to identify examples of freedom, respect, and safety in their community and explain how these contribute to the common good. Students will understand that culturally, ethnically, and racially diverse people help to shape a community.

• Civic virtues include honesty, mutual respect, cooperation, attentiveness to multiple perspectives, empathy, and courage. • Democratic principles include equality, freedom, liberty, rights, deliberation, and consideration for the common good. • Rights can include individual rights and group rights (common good). • The United States is comprised of diverse cultural groups. • Cultural groups share traditions, beliefs, religions, and holidays. • A school is made up of diverse people. • People can belong to different groups. • People speak a native language. • People share ethnicity, culture, and religion.

Rules, Processes, and Laws
D2.Civ.11.K-2. Explain how people can work together to make decisions in the classroom.
D2.Civ.12.K-2. Identify and explain how rules function in public (classroom and school) settings.
Sample C3 Indicator Connections
Sample Content Connections

Students will identify examples of how individual actions (such as volunteering or voting) and government decisions (like making laws or providing services) help create order and promote peace in their community. Students will be able to identify characteristics of effective rules and participate in a process to establish classroom rules. Students can participate in problem solving, decision making and conflict resolution within their home, school, and community. Students will understand that outcomes to conflict or disagreements based on different beliefs, culture, and values can be achieved through compromise and cooperation. Students will describe how individuals can bring about change.

• There are differences between a rule and a law. • Various people make laws/rules. • There are consequences for not following laws/rules. • Laws/rules are not the same everywhere. • Various people enforce laws/rules. • There are differences between rights (freedoms of speech and religions) and responsibilities (paying taxes, obeying the law). • People can bring about change in the classroom and/or community.

Resources

American Bar Association - Taking a Stand: Students will understand that citizens take stands on issues and explore ways to advocate for those issues. Pearl Moscowitz’s Last Stand is utilized in the lesson; it can be accessed through a video reading from the Cayton Children’s Museum.

C3 IDM - Friendship: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of early social interactions and behaviors. By investigating the compelling question “Do I have to like everyone?”, students evaluate friendship, what is a friend, how to be a friend, and how to respond when you dislike someone or they dislike you. Students will develop a deeper understanding of friendship(s). The formative performance tasks build on knowledge and skills through the course of the inquiry and help students create their own understanding of friendships and how to treat everyone fairly. Students create an evidence-based informative argument about whether or not they need to like everyone and appropriate behaviors.

C3 IDM - Global Citizen: This first grade annotated inquiry highlights the idea that even primary-age children can begin thinking about their civic roles in their communities and beyond. Those roles can be made real and vital to young children by exploring the traits or characteristics that represent responsible citizenship. Those traits – respecting others, behaving honestly, helping others, making and obeying rules and laws, being informed, and sharing needed resources – will be familiar to students through their experiences in their home and school lives.

C3 IDM - The President: This inquiry engages first graders in exploring the meaning and purpose and function of government through the compelling question “Is the president the most important person in government?” Assuming that most first graders know who the president is, this inquiry is designed to help students explore the different levels of governmental leadership and the idea that other authority figures exist in addition to the president. In learning about the levels of government and the issues each deals with, students should consider their own ideas for desired change within their communities (e.g., more recreational space, better roads, more variety in school lunches) and develop a commitment to civic participation.

iCivics - How Can Perseverance Help Me Be a Good Citizen?: The way students respond when things are challenging can be the difference between success and failure. But it’s not easy to practice a civic virtue like perseverance. This unit introduces students to behaviors they can use to work through challenges and offers the real-life examples of Wilma Rudolph and Katherine Johnson demonstrating perseverance for students to explore.
Grade 1 – People, Places, and the Environment (Draft) (Revised: November 12, 2025)
Page 7 of 24

iCivics - How Do Communities Make Good Decisions?: In this unit, students will be introduced to citizenship and leadership. Students will work together to create a classroom book on the rights and responsibilities of citizenship. Students will have the opportunity to practice citizenship by voting, recounting, and coming together for the common good.

iCivics - What Makes a Good Leader?: In this unit, students will explore leaders in their community and identify leadership traits. Students will then learn about President George Washington and identify the qualities that made people believe he would be a good first leader for the United States. Finally, students will learn about the life of Ona Judge, and examine one way in which leaders stand up for important things.

iCivics - Private i History Detectives Civic Virtues Collection: In the new Private i History Detectives Civic Virtues Collection, students learn about civic virtue champions and practice civic virtues in their own lives and in the classroom. Throughout these units, students will discover the untold stories of important and influential figures who lived out civic virtue in their own lives. They will also gain the skills they need to understand each other’s ideas and have opportunities to bring their own experiences into the learning.

KidCitizen - Children in Action: From recycling materials during World War II to wearing masks during the COVID-19 pandemic, children have helped meet community goals during times of need. In this interactive episode, students draw upon their observations and reflections to explore how children have contributed to recycling efforts in the past and present.

KidCitizen - Congress and Milk: Congress is a group of people who work together to make laws for our country. They are elected by the people to represent their interests and make decisions about important issues. We will explore one way that Congress affects children's daily life at school.

National Park Service - National Parks Legacy: Nature and Culture…NPS Protects Both!: This lesson teaches students how the National Park Service protects both nature and culture as students engage with the changing landscapes of Yellowstone national Park and Mesa Verde.

PBS Learning Media - Arthur’s Park Game: Students practice taking action to improve our world by playing ARTHUR’s Park, a digital game. In order to create a new park in an empty lot, Arthur has to make a speech to raise awareness, hold a bake sale to make money, and then equip the park. As students play each round, set in a board game format, they accumulate stars that allow them to “buy” what they need for the new park. They also recognize the importance of making a plan to achieve one’s goals.
Grade 1 – People, Places, and the Environment (Draft) (Revised: November 12, 2025)
Page 8 of 24
PBS Learning Media - My Vote Counts Lesson Plan: In this lesson from the PBS KIDS series ARTHUR, students learn about elections and to voice their preferences by voting.

PBS Learning Media - Stand Up, Sit In, Speak Out: In this lesson from the PBS KIDS series ARTHUR, students examine activism and how ordinary people can be part of powerful collective movements that bring change. Students watch “Arthur Takes a Stand” and discuss taking action against things they believe are unjust. They map out the characters’ actions, noting that multiple voices bring power and opportunities for change. Then, they listen to a story about the reasons people protest and are introduced to important movements in our country’s history. Finally, they explore different ways people take action and brainstorm a list of issues in their own community that they would like to change.

PBS Learning Media – Xavier Riddle: Talking About Life Lessons: Xavier Riddle and his friends explore values and skills such as compassion, perseverance, responsibility, and gratitude in these video clips supported with teacher materials.

PBS Learning Media – You, Me, and Community: This collection includes resources related to civics & government, geography, economics, and history. All resources are available in English, and some are available in Spanish. No student is too young to learn how to become civically engaged. Introduce young learners to basic civics concepts—including making their voice heard and exploring the process of voting.

Theme: Economic Choices
Economic Decision Making
D2.Eco.1.K-2. Explain how scarcity necessitates decision making.
D2.Eco.2.K-2. Identify the benefits and costs of making various personal decisions.
Sample C3 Indicator Connections
Sample Content Connections

Students will be able to identify choices and decisions for various uses of money (spending, saving, sharing, contributing). Students will be able to use cost-benefit analysis (i.e., weigh positives and negatives) of two choices to make a decision.

Choices and Decisions • Sources of income • Needs and wants • Identify multiple forms of U.S. money • Means of transaction • Volunteering • Different jobs in different communities • Scarcity • Opportunity costs

D2.Eco.3.K-2. Describe the skills and knowledge required to produce certain goods and services.
D2.Eco.4.K-2. Describe the goods and services that people in the local community produce and those that are produced in other communities.
D2.Eco.5.K-2. Identify prices of products in a local market.
D2.Eco.6.K-2. Explain how people earn income.
Sample C3 Indicator Connections
Sample Content Connections

Students will be able to identify prices of goods in a local market. Students will be able to describe the goods and services produced in the local community. Students will be able to identify sources of income. Students will identify how goods and services are exchanged within Vermont communities.

• Goods (maple syrup, cheddar cheese) and services (firefighter, teacher) • Sources of income • Value • People can be consumers and producers. • Local economic activities aid the national economy (e.g., VT maple syrup). • Economy is a system for using resources and distributing goods and services within a community. • Money is a means of exchange. • Trade allows consumers to have items not made in Vermont.

Global Economy
D2.Eco.14.K-2. Describe why people in one country trade goods and services with people in other countries.
D2.Eco.15.K-2. Describe products that are produced abroad and sold domestically and products that are produced domestically and sold abroad.
Sample C3 Indicator Connections
Sample Content Connections
Students will be able to explain why people in one country trade for goods in another country.

• States and countries have different resources. • Geography and environment connect in the production of goods and services. • Local goods and services export to Global markets (e.g., VT maple syrup). • Examples of products made in the United States (possible exports) • Examples of products bought here but made outside of the country (imports)
Resources

California State University - Expanding Children’s Economic World: A Curriculum Guide: This guide provides focus questions, activities, and assessments on topics such as “The Jobs People Do” and “Goods and Services.”

C3 IDM - Economic Choices: This first-grade inquiry features an investigation of economic decision making through the context of how families manage their money. In examining the costs and benefits associated with making decisions about spending and saving money, students should be able to develop an argument with evidence to answer the compelling question “What choices do we make with our money?”

C3 IDM - Economic Interdependence: This inquiry is an initial exploration into the concept of interdependence through the lens of community economics and the idea of a community as a diverse, mutually supportive web of needs and wants, workers and consumers, and problems and solutions. The compelling question, “What makes me become we?” challenges students to consider interdependence and groups to think about how a community is just a bunch of me- people living in a shared space but also a collective “we” that interacts, grows and contracts, and tries to solve issues. (This is a 2nd grade inquiry that can be adapted for younger students, as needed).
Grade 1 – People, Places, and the Environment (Draft) (Revised: November 12, 2025)
Page 12 of 24

PBS Learning Media - Needs vs. Wants: In this media-rich lesson featuring a LOOP SCOOPS video, students are introduced to the concept of “needs” vs. “wants,” and begin to consider the relationship between consumer goods and happiness.

Vermont Historical Society - My Sheep Farm Activity: William Jarvis (1770-1859) was a successful merchant and the United States Consul to Portugal and well known in both New England and Washington, DC. Jarvis played an important part in introducing Merino sheep to the United States, and subsequently in the development of the sheep herds in this country. The success of raising Merino herds in Vermont led to "merino mania."
Grade 1 – People, Places, and the Environment (Draft) (Revised: November 12, 2025)

Theme: Geography’s Influence on Culture and Environment
Geographic Representations
D2.Geo.1.K-2. Construct maps, graphs, and other representations of familiar places.
D2.Geo.2.K-2. Use maps, graphs, photographs, and other representations to describe places and the relationships and interactions that shape them.
Sample C3 Indicator Connections
Sample Content Connections
Students will understand how physical features and man-made structures are represented on a map.

Map Identifications • Physical and political maps • Physical features (e.g., roads, routes, interstates) • Continents • Oceans Map Skills • Create a map as a representation of a space (e.g., playground, neighborhood, or town common). • Identify and use map key features. • Positional word use

Human-Environment Interaction: Place, Regions, and Culture
D2.Geo.4.K-2. Explain how weather, climate, and other environmental characteristics affect people’s lives in a place or region.

• Physical environment affects the way people live and how they adapt to their physical environment (e.g., dressing for winter). • Children can take care of or hurt the environment in different ways (e.g., recycling, Green Up day, littering).

D2.Geo.7.K-2. Explain why and how people, goods, and ideas move from place to place.
D2.Geo.8.K-2. Compare how people in different types of communities use local and distant environments to meet their daily needs.

Students will examine and understand the varying communities that they belong to (e.g., family, school, town, etc.), and how they may change over time. Students will identify, respect, and explain the diverse cultures of their community and communities in the United States. Students will explain physical changes in their community over time.

Culture and Community • People in communities have multiple perspectives. • Communities can be made up of diverse social and ethnic groups. • Heritage, songs, symbols, celebrations, and folklore help to build culture. • Contributions and impact of various cultural groups in the community (e.g., variety of foods and celebrations). Physical Changes to Communities • Flooding, drought, and farming impacts (e.g., runoff, erosion) • Development

Resources

America, Our Country/Arthur: In these episodes from the PBS KIDS series ARTHUR, students examine the United States of America—the reasons it was founded, its citizens, and the symbols that represent its values.

History’s Mysteries - Why Do People Move?: This four-mystery/lesson inquiry unit helps students learn about push and pull factors, refugees, and the Great Migration by exploring primary and secondary sources to answer historical questions.
National Geographic - Exploring Maps and Models of Earth: Students compare miniature models to real things. Then they explore maps and globes as miniature versions of places and the Earth.

National Geographic - Mapping Storybooks: Students use a map and cutouts of a story's characters to follow their actions through space and time. They retell the story in their own words, using the map and positional vocabulary.

C3 IDM - Family Stories: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of their families as a way to begin understanding the concepts of past and present. By answering the compelling question “What do family stories tell us about the past?” students learn about change over time. Through the use of family artifacts (e.g., photographs, marriage licenses, family trees, keepsakes), students learn that such items can reveal information about how life in the past differs from life in the present and how their families have changed over time.

KidCitizen - Capture the Flag: By investigating primary sources displaying the American flag, we will explore the various ways people use the flag to show characteristics such as pride, loyalty, and unity for the nation. In this episode, students will engage in careful observation to identify flags and note details of the variety of places in which American flags are used.

KidCitizen - How have community helpers changed and stayed the same over time?: The importance of community helpers is a building block of civics understanding. In this episode, children investigate who community helpers are, and how they have changed over time through exploration of a rich photograph (from the Library of Congress) of a man delivering ice to a schoolhouse in 1899. Children explore the photograph by revealing it in sections, observing the details they find (See), and working with in-game character Ella to figure out what jobs the helpers are doing. Children collect elements of the photograph to their journal and use what they have collected to help them decide what the jobs are (Think), and then to connect those jobs with community helpers today (Wonder).

KidCitizen - Rosa Parks: A Proud Daughter: In this episode, children analyze a greeting card to learn about Rosa Parks and her family. The greeting card offers a familiar resource for exploring family traditions. The front of the card has an image and some simple writing. The inside of the card has a poem, and the back of the card features Rosa Parks’ handwritten note to her mother. Children observe the details of the card and analyze clues to figure out what family tradition was being celebrated. Working with in-game mentor Ella, children use parts of the card as evidence to support their ideas as they generate hypotheses about the card’s recipient, sender, and the feelings the sender wanted to express. Children explore the handwritten note on the card and practice deciphering the message by looking for familiar letters or words.
